Thank you for submitting your article "Genetic and environmental perturbations lead to regulatory decoherence" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Diethard Tautz as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal identity: Greg Gibson (Reviewer #1). The other reviewer remains anonymous.

The reviewers, and I, are convinced of the value of your approach (as one reviewer points out, this is long overdue). We do indeed have a limited understanding of the factors that shape correlations between genes and your work addresses this problem. In particular your observation that decoherent metabolites are good predictors is noteworthy, as is your successful identification of 'correlation-QTLs'. Though perhaps it is not surprising that the degree of correlation is under genetic control, it's certainly good to have that confirmed and analysed, as you have done here. Altogether, your paper represents an important advance.

I want to highlight one issue, to do with unacknowledged confounds. As one of the reviewers points out, the inclusion of expression data from multi-cellular tissues like blood is problematic, and I expected you might incorporate into your method one of the more recent analytical approaches to decompose the contributions (e.g. Nat Methods. 2017 Feb 28;14(3):218-219. doi: 10.1038/nmeth.4190). Would that improve the signal?

Separate reviews (please respond to each point):

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript on decoherence by Amanda Lee and colleagues presents a novel, and in my view long over-due, framework for considering decay of modularity of gene expression in disease conditions (among other applications). Alternative approaches describing statistical support for conservation of modules do not have resolution to individual transcripts or metabolites, so this approach holds considerable promise. I thought that the Introduction and Discussion sections were particularly insightful. I also applaud eLife for the experiment in "acceptance prior to review" and am happy to support this in this case. I hope that two more major sets of comments, followed by some minor ones, are helpful to the authors.

My first comment goes to the transparency of the description of CILP and its relationship to canalization. I think the way it is presented is overly complicated. If I am not mistaken, CILP is simply a t-test (or potentially ANOVA) of the Pearson correlation coefficients for all pairs of biomarkers in an analysis. The formula at the start of the Results section is that quantity, but then you say it is correlate with some random variable x. In actuality x is a fixed effect in all your comparisons, and it would be clearer to call it a test of association with x since it is the biomarkers that are being correlated. Furthermore, in Figure 3 you switch to the Spearman correlation, which I can see being appropriate, but is at odds with the rest of the description. Also to this point, canalization is commonly used in reference to increase in variance, which I can see could lead to de-coherence, but that is neither necessary nor sufficient, and this could be remarked upon.

My second comment has to do with the effect of unaccounted for factors on covariance. All transcriptomes and metabolomes have a high correlation structure, due to a combination of trans-acting influences, environmental influences, and mixtures of cell types. As far as I can see, the opening simulation study does not incorporate overall correlation, it only models pairwise effects due to cis-acting variation and correlation-QTL as defined by the authors. This should be acknowledged: it is extremely hard to model true transcriptional variation, but I suspect it makes a big difference. (Parenthetically, why call the cis effects b1 and b2, and the correlation effects b – another symbol for the latter would also be less confusing). Regarding the blood gene expression datasets, in the Materials and methods you consider the possibility that cell-type mixtures matter but don't find any influence of available cell counts. However, I can tell you from extensive experience that the major impact on whole blood gene expression in relation to BMI is reticulocyte count, which surprisingly is unrelated to RBC count, but if you fit Axis 2 from Preininger et al. (PMID: 23516379), renamed as Axis R in PMID: 29950172 and PMID: 30223463 and shown to strongly associate with BMI in PMID: 25300922 and PMID: 23162571 and countless other studies we've looked at, it is basically reticulocyte count. I certainly am not asking you to reference these studies (!) but do suggest you fit Axis 2 and see if it has an effect, because it is one of the major components of whole blood expression. I agree that the other Axes that correlate with B and T cell or Neutrophils only weakly associate with BMI.

Minor Comments:

Here are a few more minor comments:

Figure 2. Panel (C) described in the Legend has been removed from the version in the manuscript

LPS study: Need to reference the Fairfax et al. dataset, in the text (you don't do so until the Discussion). Also note that they describe a number of eQTL that have significantly different effects at BL, 2hr LPS, and 24hr LPS, some switching between the two exposure times. Do your correlation QTL tend to be the same, or overlap with, those instances?

Metabolic study. It is not clear from the text whether the results in Figure 3A to 3C are from t0 or from a combined analysis. I suspect just t0, please clarify. But I am also concerned that there may be inflation of the prediction of disease progression in Figure 3D due to use of the discovery dataset in the testing phase (winner's curse), especially if you used t1 and t3 in the discovery. (There will in any case be a bias due to correlations across times within individuals). I'd rather see a more robust analysis that uses a subset of the individuals and then predicts expression in the remainder – there should be sufficient sample size for this.

Subsection “Identification of disease-associated variation in metabolite correlation”, instead of stating the percentages of the subset of genes (74.4 and 25.6), state the percentages of all genes, it will still be 3:1.

Is there any indication that the transcripts that encode the enzymes that regulate the de-coherent metabolite sets are also de-coherent? I guess you may need data of both types from the same individuals, or from liver.

Regarding the correlation QTLs in NESDA, the first thing I think you should report is what fraction of them are also main effect cis-eQTL for one or the other transcript in each pair. Concerning RAP1GAP specifically, is it a trans-eQTL hotspot (I have some vague recollection that it may be, in blood). The enrichment statistics for its binding sites do not convince me at all: P<0.03 is a bit of a joke, and fibroblasts are not relevant, I don't think that result helps at all. Regarding the TF enrichment, I think you need to define what you mean by "involved in" since we now know that the locally regulated gene is usually not the closest one.

Finally, it would be interesting to know what happens to the expression in individuals who do not fall into the Healthy or MetS classes. Such ambiguous cases may have even more extreme de-coherence as they are transitional, at least at one of the time points. If the result is interesting it could be worth reporting.

Thanks for the opportunity to review such an interesting manuscript. Good luck with it.

Reviewer #2:

In this work, the authors start to investigate the potential for using the correlation between genes/metabolites as a distinct trait that may be parsable from the mean and variance of the same components. Overall, the approach seems solid albeit at points the strongest available support does not seem to be being used which does hinder the papers potential broad appeal. It is as if the need to write to clinical geneticists has slightly hamstrung the authors from really diving into the concepts that are actually very interesting and thought provoking. I have some specific questions and changes below.

On a general note, the paper is written in the general where this approach and its inferences are possibly of use in non-human systems. However, there isn't an obvious effort to discuss work in other systems, Drosophila, yeast, Arabidopsis, Maize, etc, that might influence the ideas and conclusions of this paper. There is similar work in these systems (See below) that touches on these topics and if the goal is really a broad audience they should be cited. If the goal is just a human audience than every term should be caveated by the word human, i.e. evolutionary genetics should be human evolutionary genetics, biology should be human biology, etc. Human Genetics can benefit from reading and acknowledging the work in other systems especially as Human Genetics greatly benefits from the of excellent young senior authors who come from other systems like Drosophila.

In the Introduction, the authors say "asking whether predefined sets of genes are differentially co-expressed between groups. Almost universally, these approaches are only designed for comparisons between two groups, and none can accommodate continuous predictor variables." Isn't that really only true of some approaches for the predefined set? There are groups that use the predefined sets in nested generalized models that can be extended to any complex experimental design and can include confounders and covariates. Maybe not in human genetics but at the very least in Drosophila and Arabidopsis. This should probably be tempered.

In the first section on permutation analysis (Table 1). Because of the lack of replication on individuals, VarQTLs in human genetics are a blend of all non-additive sources of variance, especially epistasis and stochasticity. Is there a difference in how epistatic variance or stochastic variance influences the claims made in this section? I ask because mechanistically it would be possible for stochastic variance to be more localized to the gene in question and not spread to other genes while epistatic variance could influence the whole network.

In the section on immunity, what was the reasoning behind limiting their analysis to the 1460 genes that were differentially expressed at the 2 hour time point? I would think that the power of the correlation approach would be that it could get more directly at the interaction term than limit itself to single timepoint selection. This choice should be explained. Especially as I wonder if this choice could create the appearance of decoherence as it does not allow for genes showing a difference at the other time points but not at 24 hours.

The RAP1GAP focus of the final section of the results has me slightly off-kilter. The authors argue for correlation being separable from other traits but then the key example is a gene with a large effect cis polymorphism. This could lead to a change in correlation by shifting genes from regulated by RAP1GAP when RAP1GAP is well expressed to no-correlation when there is low to no RAP1GAP simply because RAP1GAP is not functional. I agree that this is a real observation and does show some utility of their approach. But it would be very helpful to provide some insight of the approaches ability to get at the deeper questions that drive this manuscript. Like some examples of TF-Target correlations that were affected by trans polymorphisms. Or even metabolic gene-metabolic gene correlations that mapped to novel loci. This would help illuminate how much novel information this approach is finding.

I may be wrong but if the authors ideas about decoherence are true, shouldn't this predict that the slope in Figure 3B is less than 1? I.e. there is lower general metabolite to metabolite correlation in the y-axis (metabolic syndrome) than in the x-axis (healthy). As such, it seems that the most direct use of this data to support their conclusion would be to test if the slope is significantly lower than 1 as my interpretation of the model predicts. The rest of the information in this section seems superfluous to the idea it is trying to test.

As a small aside, there has been some work in Arabidopsis on how endogenous single gene mutants can or cannot change the correlational network in response to immune stresses similar to what is proposed in Figure 1A/B and Figure 2. These citations help to support the claim that correlation is a genetically separable trait [1,2]. I'm sure there are likely other similar citations in yeast and Drosophila.

1) Mine A, Seyfferth C, Kracher B, Berens ML, Becker D, Tsuda K: The Defense Phytohormone Signaling Network Enables Rapid, High-amplitude Transcriptional Reprogramming During Effector-Triggered Immunity. 2018.

2) Zhang W, Corwin JA, Copeland D, Feusier J, Eshbaugh R, Chen F, Atwell S, Kliebenstein DJ: Plastic transcriptomes stabilize immunity to pathogen diversity: The jasmonic acid and salicylic acid networks within the Arabidopsis/Botrytis pathosystem. Plant Cell 2017, online.

results.result: The CILP method is based on the mathematical property that the Pearson correlation coefficient equals the average element-wise product of two mean-centered and scaled traits, and can accommodate covariates and continuous predictor variables by using the product vector as an outcome in linear models.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 describe the mathematical foundation and methodological flexibility of CILP. C1 is an established mathematical fact about Pearson correlation, and C2 logically follows from the ability to use the product vector in standard linear modeling frameworks. Both claims are well-supported.

results.result: Simulation studies demonstrate that CILP has high power to detect correlation QTLs (98.19% at p<0.05, 50.91% after Bonferroni correction with effect size 0.3 and n=1000), maintains appropriate false positive rates (5.19% at p<0.05 under the null), and is robust to various confounding scenarios including eQTLs, varQTLs, and batch effects, though power decreases in the presence of strong varQTLs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C8 collectively describe simulation results validating CILP's statistical properties. The power estimates, false positive rates, and robustness to confounders are all supported by simulation data presented in Table 1 and supplementary figures. The observed 5.19% false positive rate matches the expected 5% threshold, confirming proper calibration.

results.result: LPS stimulation of human monocytes leads to widespread decoherence, with 958 gene pairs showing significant correlation changes at 2 hours (461 replicating at 24 hours), and a statistically significant bias toward loss of correlation (61% at 2hr, 73% at 24hr; p=1.05×10⁻⁷ at 2hr, p<10⁻¹⁶ at 24hr), independent of mean expression changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 describe the decoherence phenomenon in LPS-stimulated monocytes. The specific numbers of gene pairs, replication rates, percentages showing loss of correlation, and statistical significance are all supported by data from the Fairfax et al. dataset. The independence from mean expression changes (C11) addresses a potential confound and is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Metabolic syndrome is associated with widespread changes in metabolite correlation structure, with 1528 metabolite pairs showing stronger correlation in healthy individuals versus 619 showing the opposite pattern (FDR<5%), representing a 2.20-fold enrichment (p<10⁻¹⁶) for loss of correlation, affecting metabolites with varying mean expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 describe differential correlation patterns in metabolic syndrome from the YFS dataset. The specific numbers of metabolite pairs, enrichment ratios, and statistical significance are supported by the data. C19 importantly demonstrates that decoherence is not simply driven by mean expression differences, strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: Specific metabolite classes show enrichment for differential correlation in metabolic syndrome: apolipoproteins (OR=1.94, p=2.34×10⁻¹³), total cholesterol (OR=1.39, p=1.58×10⁻¹⁵), and energy metabolism molecules (OR=1.43, p=2.75×10⁻¹³) are enriched for decoherence, while fatty acids (OR=1.30, p=7.10×10⁻⁶), HDL (OR=1.18, p=1.53×10⁻⁵), and LDL (OR=1.28, p=3.58×10⁻⁶) show increased correlation in metabolic syndrome.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 describe enrichment patterns for specific metabolite classes. All odds ratios and p-values are supported by hypergeometric tests on YFS data as reported in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 3. The biological coherence of these findings (lipoproteins, cholesterol, energy metabolism) strengthens confidence in the results.

results.result: PC1 of 34 decoherent metabolites measured at baseline can predict future development of metabolic syndrome (R²=0.056, p=3.03×10⁻¹⁰, AIC=-448.40), outperforming traditional biomarkers like triglycerides (R²=0.046, p=6.32×10⁻⁹, AIC=-432.61) and metabolites with the strongest mean differences (R²=0.037, p=1.42×10⁻⁶, AIC=-422.08).
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 describe the predictive power of decoherent metabolites using longitudinal YFS data. The R² values, p-values, and AIC comparisons are all supported by the data. The comparison to traditional biomarkers (C27) and mean-difference-based approaches (C28) demonstrates the added value of the decoherence metric, though the effect sizes are modest (R²=0.056).

results.result: 484 correlation QTLs were identified in the NESDA discovery dataset (FDR<10%, involving 247 probe sets and 51 SNPs), with 304/484 replicating at Bonferroni-corrected significance and 428/484 at 10% FDR in an independent NESDA cohort, and 47/74 testable QTLs replicating in YFS with consistent effect directions (p<10⁻¹⁶).
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe the discovery and replication of correlation QTLs. The specific numbers, statistical thresholds, and replication rates are all supported by data from NESDA and YFS cohorts. The high replication rate (62.8% at Bonferroni correction, 88.4% at FDR 10%) and consistent effect directions across independent cohorts provide strong evidence for the validity of these findings.

results.result: Correlation QTLs show specific genomic architecture: 73.76% are on the same chromosome as one correlated gene, 14.57% affect both genes in cis, 11.57% act in trans on both genes, 87.81% are also cis eQTLs or varQTLs for one gene, and none affect mean or variance of both genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 describe the genomic characteristics of correlation QTLs. All percentages are supported by analysis of the physical locations and functional effects of the identified QTLs. The finding that no QTL affects both genes (C39) is important for ruling out certain confounding mechanisms and is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

results.result: Genes involved in correlation QTLs are enriched for transcription factors (1.90x, p=1.7×10⁻³), TF targets (1.52x, p=6.7×10⁻⁴), and biological processes including oxidative stress response (OR=2.21, p<10⁻¹⁶), intracellular signaling (log2 OR=1.44, p<10⁻¹⁶), and mitophagy (log2 OR=0.82, p=0.018).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 describe functional enrichments among genes with correlation QTLs. All enrichment ratios and p-values are supported by hypergeometric tests using appropriate databases (TF-target interactions, Gene Ontology). The enrichment for TFs and their targets (C40-C41) is mechanistically coherent with proposed models of how genetic variation affects co-expression.

results.result: 87.81% of correlation QTLs involve three SNPs (rs1384673, rs333170, rs829373) that are strong eQTLs for RAP1GAP, and genes in these QTLs are closer to RAP1 binding sites (p=0.04) and more likely to be bound by RAP1 in vivo (OR=2.14, p=0.03).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 describe the RAP1GAP correlation QTL hotspot. The percentage (C45) is supported by the data, and the enrichment for RAP1 binding (C46-C47) is supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data. However, the ChIP-seq data are from mouse embryonic fibroblasts rather than human blood cells, which is a limitation acknowledged by the authors but reduces confidence in the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Environmental exposures (infection and disease) lead to systematic decoherence, manifested as widespread decreases in pairwise correlation coefficients between molecular traits.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C74 state the overarching finding about decoherence. This is well-supported by the combined evidence from LPS stimulation experiments (C9-C15) and metabolic syndrome analyses (C16-C19), which both show statistically significant biases toward loss of correlation following environmental perturbations.

results.result: Decoherent metabolites are better predictors of future metabolic syndrome development than traditional biomarkers, and decoherence at the molecular level is associated with disease risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C85 describe the predictive value of decoherent metabolites. This is supported by the longitudinal analysis (C26-C28) showing that PC1 of decoherent metabolites outperforms traditional biomarkers. However, the effect sizes are modest (R²=0.056), and the clinical utility would require further validation.

results.result: Correlation between mRNA transcripts is under genetic control, as demonstrated by mapping hundreds of correlation QTLs, filling a gap in understanding the genetic basis of differential co-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C51, and C90 state the main finding about genetic control of correlation. This is well-supported by the discovery of 484 correlation QTLs (C29-C34) with high replication rates across independent cohorts. The claim that this fills a gap (C90) is supported by the limited prior literature on this topic.

results.result: The RAP1GAP correlation QTL hotspot is generated because genotype controls whether RAP1 and its targets are constitutively 'on' or 'off', with variation in RAP1 activity only modulating target gene expression within the 'on' genotype.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 proposes a specific mechanistic model for the RAP1GAP hotspot. While this hypothesis is consistent with the observed data (C45-C47) and is illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3, it remains speculative. The ChIP-seq data supporting RAP1 binding are from mouse fibroblasts rather than human blood, and no direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanism is provided. Additional experiments would be needed to confirm this model.

results.result: Decoherence may play a role in disease, potentially representing decanalization at the molecular level where formerly co-regulated molecules become dysregulated, and decoherent metabolites could serve as biomarkers.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C84, C86, and C87 make speculative statements about the role of decoherence in disease and its potential clinical applications. While the association between decoherence and disease is well-documented (C48, C74), the causal role and mechanistic interpretation in terms of decanalization (C84) remain speculative. The biomarker potential (C87) is suggested by C26-C28 but would require extensive validation before clinical application.

results.result: Co-expression analysis is important for understanding regulatory changes in disease and evolution, and decanalization theory suggests that gene regulatory networks evolve under stabilizing selection but can be disrupted by novel environments or mutations, potentially explaining the rise of non-communicable diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 and C70-C73 provide background context from the literature about co-expression analysis and decanalization theory. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations to prior work and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide the conceptual framework for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Previous approaches for studying differential co-expression have limitations: they typically compare population-level statistics between groups, cannot test continuous predictors, and may not account for individual-level covariates, making it difficult to identify individual-specific factors affecting co-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 critique previous methodological approaches. These critiques are supported by citations to prior work and logical analysis of the limitations of existing methods. The claims accurately describe the methodological gap that CILP aims to fill, though the characterization of all previous methods as having these limitations may be somewhat overstated.

results.result: The relationship between genetic variation and co-expression is largely unexplored, though one proposed mechanism involves SNPs disrupting transcription factor binding sites, and alternative mechanisms may exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 discuss potential mechanisms for genetic effects on co-expression. C63 describes a hypothetical mechanism, C64 notes this has been proposed with some empirical support (citing appropriate literature), and C65-C66 note the limited exploration of this topic. These claims are well-supported and provide context for the novelty of the correlation QTL findings.

results.result: Similar patterns of biased loss of correlation have been observed in other contexts (cognitive impairment, aging, cancer), and the observed decoherence represents an extension of decanalization models, though traditionally decanalization has been conceptualized as increased variance rather than changed correlation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C83 place the current findings in the context of prior observations and decanalization theory. The citations to similar patterns in other systems (C75-C77) are appropriate, and the discussion of decanalization theory (C79-C83) accurately represents the literature while noting the novel interpretation of decanalization as correlation change rather than variance change.

results.result: Prior work on differential co-expression has focused on environmental contrasts while the genetic basis has received less attention, though recent studies by Nath et al., Lukowski et al., and van der Wijst et al. point toward genetic control of co-expression, and CILP provides tools to probe this further.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C95 review prior work on genetic effects on co-expression and position CILP as advancing this area. The characterization of prior work is accurate and supported by appropriate citations. The claim that CILP provides additional tools (C95) is supported by the methodological advantages described in C2 and demonstrated in the correlation QTL analyses.

results.result: Future priorities include mapping correlation QTLs across environments and elucidating mechanisms, though genome-wide screens will require large sample sizes due to multiple testing burden; CILP's power increases with sample size, unlike methods comparing group-level statistics.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 discuss future directions and limitations. The statements about future priorities (C96-C97) are reasonable research directions. The computational burden of genome-wide screens (C98-C99) is a logical inference. The claim about CILP's power scaling with sample size (C100) is supported by the simulation results, and the comparison to other methods (C101) is a valid statistical observation.

results.result: The study focused on humans due to data availability but builds on model system work; CILP could be useful with multi-parent populations, for studying GxE effects on correlation, and in ecological contexts, as questions about correlation variation are central to many fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C111 discuss the scope of the current study and potential future applications. The rationale for focusing on humans (C102) is explicit, the connection to model system work (C103-C104) is supported by appropriate citations, and the proposed future applications (C105-C109) are reasonable extensions of the method. The broad applicability claim (C111) is speculative but plausible given the generality of the approach.

results.result: Previous work has found evidence for convergence of trans eQTL effects on RAP1GAP in whole blood, and RAP1 has been implicated in insulin resistance, inflammation, and obesity.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 cite prior work on RAP1GAP and RAP1. These claims are supported by appropriate citations and provide biological context for the RAP1GAP correlation QTL hotspot findings. The relevance to metabolic disease (C69) is particularly pertinent given the focus on BMI-associated genes.
